title: Async, promises, the event loop
blurb: The event loop, microtasks, promise combinators, and the five ways async/await quietly goes wrong. Expect at least one of these in every JavaScript interview.

questions.q: What order do these log?
questions.why: Synchronous code first (a, d). Then the microtask queue drains completely (c). Only then does the event loop take a macrotask — the timer (b). Microtasks always beat timers.
questions.asked: The definitive event-loop question. Getting the order right matters less than being able to say why.

questions.q: What is the difference between the task queue and the microtask queue?
choices: Microtasks drain fully after each task, before the next task or render
Microtasks run on a separate thread
Tasks are for I/O, microtasks for CPU work
questions.why: Promise callbacks and queueMicrotask go on the microtask queue and run to exhaustion after the current task. setTimeout, I/O and events are tasks. An infinite chain of microtasks starves rendering entirely.
questions.asked: The follow-up is 'so can a promise chain block the UI?' — yes, it can.

questions.q: What is wrong with this?
choices: It runs the requests one at a time — for 100 ids that is 100 round trips in series
`await` is not allowed inside a for...of loop
It will throw on the first request
questions.why: It is correct but serial. If the requests are independent, `await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchUser))` runs them concurrently. Serial is right only when each call depends on the previous one, or you need to limit load.
questions.asked: The most common real async performance bug, and it looks completely reasonable.

questions.q: What does `Promise.all` do when one promise rejects?
choices: Rejects immediately with that error; the others keep running but their results are discarded
Waits for all of them and returns an array of results and errors
Skips the failed one and resolves with the rest
questions.why: all is fail-fast. Nothing is cancelled — the other requests still complete, you just never see them. Use Promise.allSettled when you want every outcome.
questions.asked: Then: 'when would you use allSettled instead?' — dashboards where one failed widget shouldn't blank the page.

questions.q: Which combinator resolves with the first promise to FULFIL, ignoring rejections until all fail?
questions.why: any waits for the first success and only rejects (with an AggregateError) if every input rejects. race settles on the first promise to settle either way — including a rejection.
questions.asked: race vs any is a clean way to check whether someone has actually used these rather than heard of them.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: An async function always returns a promise, wrapping whatever you return. To see the value you must await it or use .then.
questions.asked: The origin of 'why is my function returning a Promise instead of the data?'

questions.q: What happens to a rejected promise nobody handles?
choices: An unhandled rejection — Node can crash the process, browsers log an error
questions.why: Since Node 15 an unhandled rejection terminates the process by default. In a browser it fires the `unhandledrejection` event and logs. Either way it is a bug, not a warning.
questions.asked: Especially in Node: 'why does our service exit with no stack trace?'

questions.q: Why does this not catch the error?
choices: forEach ignores the returned promises, so the try block finishes before any save runs
questions.why: forEach discards return values, so nothing is awaited and rejections escape as unhandled. Use `for...of` with await for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(items.map(save))` for concurrent.
questions.asked: One of the top five real-world async bugs, and it looks fine in review.

questions.q: What order do these log?
questions.why: An async function runs synchronously up to the first await. `await null` still yields to the microtask queue, so the rest of the function is queued and 3 logs first.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know that `await` always defers, even on a non-promise.

questions.q: How do you cancel an in-flight `fetch`?
choices: Pass an AbortController's signal, then call controller.abort()
You cannot; you must ignore the result
questions.why: `fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal })` — aborting rejects the promise with an AbortError. This is the correct fix for the React fetch race and for a search-as-you-type box.
questions.asked: The practical follow-up to 'how would you stop stale results overwriting fresh ones?'

questions.q: What is wrong with retrying a failed request on every error?
choices: Non-idempotent requests may be applied twice, and 4xx errors will never succeed on retry
questions.why: Retry transient failures — network errors, 429, 502/503/504 — with exponential backoff and jitter. Do not retry 400 or 404; they will fail identically. And retrying a non-idempotent POST can create two orders.
questions.asked: A very common backend question. The strong answer mentions idempotency keys.

questions.q: What does 'exponential backoff with jitter' mean?
choices: Each retry waits roughly twice as long as the last, plus a random offset
Retry twice as many times each round
Wait until the server sends a retry header
questions.why: Doubling the delay stops you hammering a struggling service. The random jitter stops every client retrying in lockstep and re-creating the spike — the 'thundering herd'.
questions.asked: The jitter half is the part that distinguishes a considered answer.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: Each .then returns a new promise resolved with that handler's return value. The first handler returns nothing, so the second receives undefined. Forgetting to return inside a .then is a classic chain bug.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand that .then transforms rather than observes.

questions.q: Where does the error go?
choices: catch handles it and 'after' still runs — catch returns a fulfilled promise
questions.why: A catch handler that returns normally puts the chain back into the fulfilled state, so anything after it continues. That is how you recover with a fallback value.

questions.q: Does `fetch` reject on a 404?
choices: No — it only rejects on network failure; check `response.ok` yourself
Only in Node, not in the browser
questions.why: fetch resolves as long as it got a response. A 404 or 500 is a successful HTTP exchange as far as it is concerned. This surprises people coming from axios, which does throw.
questions.asked: Extremely common, because it produces a bug where errors show up as 'undefined is not a function' deep in render code.

questions.q: What is bounded concurrency and why would you want it?
choices: Running at most N async operations at once, to avoid overwhelming a service or exhausting sockets
Limiting how long a promise can take
questions.why: `Promise.all` over 10,000 items opens 10,000 connections at once and gets you rate-limited or out of file descriptors. A pool keeps N in flight and starts the next as each finishes.
questions.asked: Comes up whenever you say 'I process a batch of records'.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: The promise executor runs synchronously the moment you construct the promise — so A logs first. The .then callback is a microtask, so it runs after the current script (C).
questions.asked: People assume the executor is deferred. It is not.

questions.q: How do you add a timeout to a promise that has no timeout option?
choices: Promise.race it against a promise that rejects after N ms
You cannot without changing the underlying call
questions.why: race settles on whichever finishes first. Note the original operation is not cancelled by this — for fetch, combine it with an AbortController (or use AbortSignal.timeout).
questions.asked: The good answer adds 'but race doesn't cancel the slow one'.

questions.q: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism in JavaScript?
choices: JS is concurrent on one thread by interleaving; true parallelism needs Workers or child processes
Parallelism happens automatically on multi-core machines
questions.why: The event loop interleaves waiting operations on a single thread — great for I/O, useless for CPU work. A tight loop blocks everything; move that to a Worker (browser) or worker_threads / another process (Node).
questions.asked: Then: 'what would you do about a slow CPU-bound endpoint?'

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: `return await` inside try/catch keeps the rejection inside the function, so the catch runs. Writing plain `return Promise.reject(...)` would hand the rejection to the caller and skip the local catch.
questions.asked: A genuinely subtle one — 'return await' is not always redundant.

questions.q: What is a race condition in a UI data fetch?
choices: A slower earlier request resolves after a faster later one and overwrites fresh data with stale data
Two components rendering at the same time
Two users editing the same record
questions.why: Type 'ab' fast: the request for 'a' can land after the request for 'ab'. Fix by aborting the previous request, or by ignoring any response that is not for the current input.
questions.asked: The React version of this is an entire interview question on its own.

questions.q: What does `queueMicrotask` do that `setTimeout(fn, 0)` does not?
choices: Runs before the next render and before any pending timer
questions.why: queueMicrotask schedules on the microtask queue, which drains before the event loop moves on. setTimeout(fn, 0) is a task and is also clamped to about 4ms after nesting.

questions.q: In Node, what does `process.nextTick` do relative to promises?
choices: Its queue is drained before the promise microtask queue
It runs on a worker thread
questions.why: Node keeps a separate nextTick queue that is processed before promise microtasks. Recursively calling nextTick can starve the event loop entirely.
questions.asked: A Node-specific depth check. Fine to say you avoid nextTick in application code.

questions.q: What is wrong with this error handling?
choices: It swallows every failure identically, so a bug and a missing record look the same
catch cannot be used without a parameter
await is not allowed in try
questions.why: A blanket catch hides programming errors alongside expected ones. Catch the failures you can actually handle, log the rest, and let genuinely unexpected errors surface.
questions.asked: Usually phrased as 'what would you change in this code review?'

questions.q: What does an async generator let you do?
choices: `for await...of` over values that arrive over time, like pages of an API
questions.why: It is the clean way to express pagination: the consumer writes `for await (const item of allUsers())` and never sees the page cursor at all.

questions.q: Two `await`s in a row, on independent operations. What is the fix?
questions.code:
const user = await getUser(id);
const settings = await getSettings(id);
questions.why: As written, the second request does not start until the first finishes, doubling latency for no reason. Promise.all starts both immediately.
questions.asked: A near-guaranteed follow-up to any async question, and easy to spot once you look for it.

questions.q: What is the state machine of a promise?
choices: pending → fulfilled or rejected, once, permanently
pending → running → done, and it can restart
It can move between fulfilled and rejected freely
questions.why: A promise settles exactly once and keeps that result forever. That is why calling resolve twice does nothing, and why awaiting the same promise repeatedly returns the cached value rather than re-running the work.
questions.asked: It explains why a promise is not a substitute for an observable or an event stream.

questions.q: Why does `setInterval` drift?
choices: It schedules by wall clock but the callback can be delayed, and delays accumulate
It runs on a different thread
questions.why: If the main thread is busy, the callback runs late — and the next tick is scheduled from that late point, or fires immediately. For a clock or stopwatch, compute elapsed time from a start timestamp instead of counting ticks.
questions.asked: A concrete question with an obviously right answer: never accumulate time by counting intervals.

questions.q: What does `await` do to a non-promise value?
choices: Wraps it, yields to the microtask queue, then resumes with the value
Returns it synchronously with no delay
Converts it to a promise that never resolves
questions.why: `await 1` still defers the rest of the function by at least one microtask tick. That is why sprinkling awaits on synchronous values changes execution order.

questions.q: You need to process 5,000 records against a rate-limited API. What is the right shape?
choices: A worker pool of N concurrent workers pulling from the queue, with backoff on 429
A for loop with await, one at a time
setTimeout with a fixed delay between each
questions.why: Promise.all floods the API. A serial loop is needlessly slow. A bounded pool keeps throughput high while respecting the limit, and honouring 429 / Retry-After keeps you from getting blocked.
questions.asked: A realistic design question — the answer shows whether you have done batch work in production.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: 1 is synchronous. The top-level `await 0` queues the remainder as a microtask — but queueMicrotask was already queued first, so 3 runs, then 4. The timer is a task and comes last.

questions.q: Why should a promise-returning function never also take a callback?
choices: Dual APIs double the error paths and callers inevitably use both
questions.why: Node's older APIs did this and it produced functions that could both reject and call back with an error. Pick one contract; use util.promisify at the boundary if you must wrap old code.
